text.p: House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich will face one of the biggest challenges of his political career in November, even though his own bid for re-election seems fairly safe, analysts say.

The 53-year-old Republican incumbent is expected to defeat Democratic challenger Michael Coles in Georgia's 6th Congressional District, a suburban area north of Atlanta with one of the most conservative electorates in the country.

The big gamble for Gingrich lies instead in the Republican Party's national struggle with Democrats for control of the U.S. House of Representatives. What's at stake for him in that contest is not only his position as speaker but, potentially, his very future as a political figure.
"He would be in a very perilous situation if the Republicans lost control of the House," said Merle Black, a political scientist at Emory University in Atlanta.

"He would be the first person that his critics within the Republican Party would blame for the defeat, as one of the most unpopular politicians in the country and with that unpopularity being used against other Republican (House) candidates. At some point, he would probably resign."

Republicans hold a 235-198 seat advantage in the House. But with President Bill Clinton clinging stubbornly to a double-digit lead over Republican challenger Bob Dole, Democrats are using the momentum of the presidential campaign to wage a pitched battle for the 20 House seats they need to reclaim the Congressional chamber.

With barely three weeks to go until the election, analysts said the fight for the House appeared to be a toss-up, partly because Democratic candidates successfully exploited voter disaffection with Gingrich and his reform plans for popular federal programmes such as Medicare.
Gingrich continued to shrug off the possibility of defeat the with an air of terse but resolute optimism.
"We'll gain seats -- plus six to plus 23," he told Reuters during a campaign stop in his home district over the weekend.
And as to his own future, should the House race turn against the Republicans, he said: "I think that's now so remote a possibility, I don't even worry about it."
Two years ago Gingrich led a campaign assault against the Democrats that put the Republican Party in charge of both the House and Senate for the first time in 40 years.
The victory propelled him to the forefront of the American political landscape and briefly fanned speculation about a possible run for the White House.

But his meteoric rise has been clouded by controversy and a series of missteps -- an ill-fated budget standoff with Clinton, an ongoing House ethics investigation, voter fears about Medicare reforms and public dislike for his confrontational style of politics.

Some political experts believed Gingrich, a former history professor with an affinity for the British parliamentary system, would see a Republican defeat in the House as a referendum vote on his own party leadership and step down.
"He also would be facing an ethics probe in the hands of Democrats. I don't think he's going to stick around for that," said Emory University's Black.

Gingrich hoped to recapture his campaign laurels of 1994 by using his influence to electrify the party faithful, particularly in conservative districts where Republican House candidates face a close race.
A whirlwind travel schedule took him to 117 House districts during this election cycle. And with Election Day drawing near, his agenda called for at least another dozen campaign stops.

Gingrich aides said the tour raised $8.7 million in campaign contributions for Republicans despite claims that some candidates would rather distance themselves from the speaker in the interests of their own survival.

"If there's going to be a fairly light turnout in the presidential context, then someplace where the speaker comes in and raises the Republican turnout by two or three percentage points -- that could make a hell of a difference," said Richard Galen, communications director for Gingrich's political office in Washington.
